title: Festivals differ
hook: Vesak, Hanamatsuri, Saga Dawa: one birth, many calendars

segments.voice: Yesterday, robes and colors: saffron, maroon, gray and black, and the rice fields of Magadha sewn into each. Your line was the robe's color.

A small shrine sits on a temple step, its roof covered in fresh flowers. Inside stands a statue of a baby, no taller than a teacup, one hand pointing up to the sky and one down to the earth. A line of children waits with a bamboo ladle. One by one, each dips it in a bowl of sweet tea and pours it gently over the baby's head. Then they giggle and drink a little themselves. It's a birthday party. The guest of honor was born a very long time ago.
screen: `A SHRINE COVERED IN FLOWERS.` → `A BABY POINTING UP AND DOWN.` → `SWEET TEA ON HIS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Why pour water on a baby statue? A Pali discourse, the Discourse on Wonderful and Marvelous Qualities, tells of the Buddha's birth: the newborn stands, takes seven steps, looks out over the quarters and speaks. And two streams of water appear from the sky, one cool and one warm, to bathe him and his mother. The children with the ladle retell that moment with their hands. So the birth is shared. The days are not. First, Vesak, which you met back in year one, kept by Theravada communities in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia on a full moon in the month of Vesakha. Theravada tradition marks three things on that one day: the birth, the awakening and the passing away. Lanterns, white clothes, temple visits, food given freely. Second, Hanamatsuri, the flower festival, the scene you just heard. In Japan it honors the birth alone, the flowered shrine recalling the garden at Lumbini where tradition says he was born. Korea, China and Vietnam keep their own birthday celebrations by their own calendars, with lanterns and the same bathing of the baby. Third, Saga Dawa, a whole month of practice for Tibetan communities. Its full-moon day honors the awakening and the passing, and in some reckonings the birth as well. People walk circuits around holy places, give to those in need, and some avoid eating meat for the month. So the same birth may be celebrated on several days in one year, by communities that each have good reasons for their count.
screen: `TWO STREAMS OF WATER.` · `VESAK: THREE MOMENTS, ONE DAY.` · `HANAMATSURI: THE FLOWER FESTIVAL.` · `SAGA DAWA: A WHOLE MONTH.` · then, large: `ONE BIRTH, MANY DAYS.`

segments.voice: Call up the little shrine of flowers and the children with the ladle. On each out-breath, picture a little water poured, one cool stream, one warm, over a birth you're grateful for: your own, a child's, a friend's, anyone's.
Festivals differ. Vesak, Hanamatsuri, Saga Dawa: different days, different customs, all honoring the same life. Today's word.
Your line: one birth, many days. Nobody here is late to the party; they just keep different calendars. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists keep Vesak with temple visits, lanterns and giving; in Japan, Hanamatsuri is kept by pouring sweet tea over a baby Buddha statue in a flower-covered shrine; Tibetan Buddhists keep Saga Dawa as a month of practice, giving and circling holy places.

chat.says: Why do Buddhists celebrate the Buddha's birthday on different days?
options: Each keeps its own calendar: Vesak, Hanamatsuri and Saga Dawa honor one birth.
Because each school honors a different Buddha's birth, not the same one.
Because the early texts never mention his birth, so each picked a day.
chat.meaning: The birth is shared; the days are not. Vesak marks birth, awakening and passing; Hanamatsuri, the birth alone; Saga Dawa is a month of practice.
